description: Sanbosi es un equipo apasionado por la tecnología y la ciencia, integrado por estudiantes y profesores de la FET. Nos interesa desarrollar ideas y soluciones mediante software, inteligencia artificial, automatización, robótica y otras tecnologías. Buscamos aprender, innovar y trabajar en equipo, uniendo diferentes conocimientos para convertir ideas en proyectos con impacto.
summary:
SANBOSI Space Health is a tool that helps astronauts look after their health during space missions.

We developed a software prototype: a smartwatch (a web page in this version) that tracks pulse, oxygen, temperature, sleep and radiation, and that astronauts can talk to. Its data goes to a dashboard for the doctor on board, with a 3D human figure that shows how each part of the body is doing. In the prototype, vital signs are simulated.

The tool compares every reading with what is normal for that person and with NASA limits. If something changes, it warns within seconds and explains what is happening and what to do, without waiting for Earth. It uses real NASA data: air and radiation from the International Space Station and blood tests of four crew members from a real mission.

This matters because, on the way to Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes, and astronauts need to know right away if their health is at risk.
details:
SANBOSI Space Health monitors each astronaut’s health and warns them on board, within seconds, when something changes. It works in three parts. The astronaut wears a watch that measures pulse, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, skin temperature, breathing, sleep and movement, and that they can talk to: they just say “Hey Sanbosi”. Every 2 seconds the watch sends its data to a server inside the spacecraft that works without internet. The server discards poor-quality readings and compares each value with two references: NASA health limits (for example, cabin CO₂ above 3 mmHg or blood oxygen below 94%) and what is normal for that person. If something goes out of range, it issues an alert that explains what changed, what to do and which NASA health risk is involved. The flight surgeon sees everything on a dashboard with a 3D human figure: touching each part of the body shows its status. Critical alerts and summaries travel to Earth over a network that survives signal outages.

In the prototype, the watch is a web page and the vital signs are simulated. Everything else uses real data: cabin air and radiation from the International Space Station, solar protons from the GOES satellites (NOAA) and the blood tests of the four Inspiration4 crew members, published by NASA, which serve as the medical record of the demo astronauts.

The main benefit is time: astronauts get alerts within seconds instead of waiting up to 22 minutes for an answer from Earth. Comparing each person with their own normal reduces false alarms. The flight surgeon understands why each alert was raised, and the ground team receives summaries sorted by priority even when the signal is lost.

We hope the idea serves long missions to the Moon and Mars, where crews will have to look after themselves. The next step is to build the first physical version with a commercial smartwatch (Galaxy Watch5 or later) and a Teviso BG51 radiation module on the strap, validate the thresholds with health professionals and test it in a space analog. On Earth, the same idea can help people who work far from a doctor, such as in rural areas, mines or remote stations.

To build it we used Python 3 (Starlette, Uvicorn, SQLite, NumPy and SciPy) for the server; JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the watch and dashboards, with Three.js for the 3D figure and the browser’s speech features; Ollama with the Llama 3.2 3B model as a local assistant; a delay-tolerant networking (DTN) emulator based on Grover and Ponce (2026); and Remotion for the video. The proposed hardware is a Samsung Galaxy Watch5 or later with the Samsung Health Sensor SDK, a Teviso BG51 radiation sensor and an ESP32-C3 microcontroller.

What makes it creative is that it brings together the body, the environment and radiation, which today are measured separately. It also uses the voice as a health sensor: tone, pauses and speech rate help detect fatigue or stress, a research gap NASA has open. It works on board first without depending on Earth, every alert is linked to an official NASA risk, and the radiation module sits on the watch strap.

The team took safety into account: the system supports decisions but does not diagnose, and the team’s health members reviewed the indicators. We also considered privacy (data stays on board and only summaries travel to Earth), communication delays and outages, false alarms, hands-free use through voice, language (Spanish and English) and the fact that a flight version would need radiation-hardened components.
